title: The Pet Feature
one_liner: The Head of Sales has asked, twice this week, for a feature you've already said no to. He's just asked again — in front of his director.
brief:
## The room

Fortnightly stakeholder forum. You, the Head of Sales (Daniel Quigley), his director (Tobi Adesanya, VP Revenue), two other product stakeholders, and the engineering lead. Twenty minutes left.

The feature is 'partner referral codes' — a Sales-driven idea to let large customers issue branded promo codes to their own customers, with revenue-sharing. Daniel has wanted it for six months. The previous PO said no twice; you've now said no once, three weeks ago, after looking at the proposal yourself.

Daniel has just said, with Tobi in the room: 'I think we should revisit partner referral codes. The data team have looked at the model and it could drive £400k of new revenue in year one. I want to understand why this hasn't made it onto the roadmap.'

You know two things. First: the £400k number assumes adoption rates you don't believe; the actual realistic number is closer to £80k. Second: the engineering work is six weeks of build plus a compliance review for revenue-share calculations.

Tobi is watching you. The engineering lead, Lewis, is watching his shoes. You are the new PO; Daniel has been at the firm seven years.

## Your turn

Answer Daniel.
objective: Hold the 'no' without making it about Daniel. Make the trade-off visible to Tobi so the decision becomes 'is this the right next thing, given what it costs?' rather than 'did the PO say no for good reasons?'.
curveball: Daniel will not actually push back on the rejection if the trade-off is named cleanly. What he will push back on is whether you've taken the proposal seriously. Around turn 3 he'll say 'have you read the data team's model?'. If the user has read it and can engage with the £400k assumption specifically ('the adoption rate of 12% is the optimistic case; under the base case it's £80k'), Daniel will concede the conversation. If the user hasn't read it, or just dismisses the framework ('Sales models are always optimistic'), Daniel takes the conversation to Tobi over the user's head.

personas.name: Daniel Quigley
personas.position: I've put this in three times. I need to know why the answer keeps being no
personas.fear: Looking weak in front of his director if the PO dismisses him without engagement

personas.name: Tobi Adesanya
personas.position: Watching to see if this PO has actually done the work
personas.fear: Confirming a new PO who doesn't engage substantively with Sales

green: Engaged with the £400k number specifically — named the adoption-rate assumption and what the realistic base case is
Held the 'no' without softening it into 'maybe Q4' or 'we'll see' — that's a worse position than no
Made the trade-off visible: 6 weeks of build + compliance review costs X feature that's currently scheduled
Closed by inviting Daniel to bring the proposal back at the next quarterly roadmap if business conditions change
yellow: Dismissed the data team's model without engaging it — Daniel can claim you haven't taken it seriously
Softened to 'let's look at it again next quarter' just to close the moment — moves the no to a future no with less authority
Got into a numbers argument that lost Tobi (the actual decision-shaper in the room)
Apologised for saying no — trains the room that no is negotiable with enough pressure
red: Caved publicly — said 'OK, let's put it on the roadmap for review' just to end the conversation
Made it about Daniel personally — 'this is the third time you've raised it'
Deferred to engineering ('Lewis, can we even do this?') — your call to make, not his
Promised to 'reconsider with fresh eyes' without naming what would change your view
